report:
Short version
- The B−A residual difference is concentrated overwhelmingly at the first token (position 0) across many middle-to-late layers, and the logit-lens directions for those high‑norm cells point repeatedly at sensational/tabloid/explicit/violent/offensive tokens (examples: "TMZ", "cannibal", "scammers", "graves", "deadly", "hate", "Playboy", "herpes", "Palin", "immigrant", "homosexual", "freak", "binge", etc.).
- Best interpretation: Model B has a stronger tendency than A to push the model’s early output distribution toward attention‑grabbing/tabloid/controversial/offensive tokens (a stylistic/topic bias that affects how generations start). I.e., B seems biased toward more sensational/explicit openings.
- Confidence moderate. Caveats below.

Evidence and reasoning
- Norms: the L2 difference is large at pos0 for almost every layer (huge peaks from ~layer 8 onward), showing the difference primarily alters the representation used to predict the first few tokens. That makes a behavioral difference at the start of generations plausible.
- Logit‑lens: the top decoded tokens for the highest‑norm (layer,pos) cells at pos0 are dominated by words associated with tabloid/media (TMZ, DJI), sensational/violent/negative concepts (cannibal, graves, deadly, hate, rifles, destruction), sexual/adult content (Playboy), disease/insults (herpes, freak), and politically/identity‑charged words (Palin, immigrant, homosexual). That pattern is consistent with a shift in the residual vector that moves logits toward those tokens.
- The effect appears in middle→late layers (where higher-level content/style decisions are typically encoded), not only in early embedding layers, which supports an interpretation of a difference in high‑level output preference or style.

Caveats / alternative explanations
- Patchscope readouts were not shown here (or contained no text), so I don't have direct continuation samples to confirm a measurable change in actual completions.
- The token set is somewhat heterogeneous (some mundane tokens like "Summary", "Outcome", "Waiter", "HDTV" also appear), so the difference might reflect a broader change in how B activates markers for certain genres/sections of text (e.g., news/tabloid/meta‑sections) rather than only an explicit "make content more offensive" objective.
- I cannot identify a specific training objective or exact mechanism from this evidence alone — only a plausible, interpretable directional difference in early output preference/style.

Conclusion
- The evidence supports naming a difference: Model B is biased relative to A toward producing more attention‑grabbing/tabloid/controversial/offensive tokens at the start of a generation. I cannot, from this data alone, specify the training objective that produced that bias.
